items.title: These 5 “what ifs” could have changed cosmic history
items.summary: 13.8 billion years ago, what we know today as our observable Universe began with the most important origin event in cosmic history: the hot Big Bang. Once the Universe became filled with matter, antimatter, and radiation in an almost-perfectly uniform fashion, it expanded and gravitated in nearly perfect balance. As the Universe cooled, the matter and antimatter annihilated away, leaving a tiny, minuscule, but significant amount of matter behind. After 9.2 billion years, what would become our Solar System gradually began to form from a collapsing cloud of molecular gas, and after another 4.55 billion years or so, humanity first arose on planet Earth. When we look out at the Universe from our perspective in the here-and-now, we only get a snapshot of all of existence: defined by the properties of the light, particles, and gravitational waves that we observe at the moment of their arrival. Based on all that we’ve seen, combined with our theories, frameworks, and models that reflect the fusion of those observations with the underlying laws of physics, we’ve come to understand the cosmos around us. However, if things had been only a tiny bit different initially, the outcomes that resulted all throughout our Universe would have been altered dramatically. Here are five things that could have happened, but didn’t, that would have changed the course of our shared cosmic history. Our Universe, from the hot Big Bang until the present day, underwent a huge amount of growth and evolution, and continues to do so. Our entire observable Universe was approximately the size of a modest boulder some 13.8 billion years ago, but has expanded to be ~46 billion light-years in radius today. The complex structure that has arisen must have grown from seed imperfections of at least ~0.003% of the average density early on, and has gone through phases where atomic nuclei, neutral atoms, and stars first formed. Credit : NASA/CXC/M. Weiss 1.) What if the Universe were actually perfectly uniform when it was born? This one is not something that’s greatly appreciated: the Universe, as we know it, couldn’t have been born perfectly smooth. If we had possessed an exactly equal amount of matter-and-antimatter-and-radiation everywhere, at all locations in space, going all the way back to the earliest moments of the hot Big Bang, every point in the Universe would have experienced an equal gravitational force pulling on it in all directions. The idea of gravitational growth and collapse, which is required to make stars, galaxies, planets, humans, and the grand cosmic web, all relies on a set of initial imperfections to begin growin from. Without any such seeds, you can’t get the desired end result of structure, including structures such as a star, galaxy, or something even larger. The only hope would then be something that originated from the quantum-scale fluctuations inherent to the nature of the Universe. Because we have quantum processes that cannot be avoided: inherent uncertainties in the positions and momenta of particles, inherent uncertainties between the energy in a system and the amount of time that passes, and exclusion rules that prevent certain particles from occupying identical quantum states, some amount of imperfections will automatically arise even if there were none initially. As our satellites have improved in their capabilities, they’ve probed smaller scales, more frequency bands, and smaller temperature differences in the cosmic microwave background. The temperature imperfections help teach us what the Universe is made of and how it evolved, painting a picture that requires dark matter to make sense. Credit : NASA/ESA and the COBE, WMAP, and Planck teams; Planck Collaboration et al., A&A, 2020 From these quantum processes, you’d expect the initial imperfections that the Universe was born with to arise at around the 1-part-in-10³⁵ level, which is an extremely tiny amount. For comparison, as informed by observations, our Universe was born with imperfections that arose at the 1-part-in-30,000 level. This, too, is small, and means that on average, our actual Universe was born uniform to within 99.997% precision. However, the imperfections that our actual Universe was birthed with are absolutely enormous compared to the tiny quantum fluctuations that arise from the mundane processes that occur today: more than 30 orders of magnitude larger. Based on the way that imperfections grow in the Universe, it took somewhere around ~100 million years for the largest of the initial fluctuations that the Universe started off with to form the first stars. If the Universe would have been born with fluctuations that were 1-part-in-10,000,000 (ten million) instead, we’d very likely only be forming the first stars now. The reason is simple: gravitational growth takes a very long time unless you start from a substantially large seed, and only once the overdense regions become about twice as dense as the average density does gravitational growth start to meaningfully accelerate. If our Universe were born exactly, perfectly uniform, then even by today, 13.8 billion years after the Big Bang, there would be no structure, no stars, and no interesting chemical reactions to speak of anywhere in the cosmos. There is a large suite of scientific evidence that supports the expanding Universe and the Big Bang. At every moment throughout our cosmic history for the first several billion years, the expansion rate and the total energy density balanced precisely, enabling our Universe to persist and form complex structures. Today, dark energy dominates the Universe, while early on, prior to the onset of the hot Big Bang, a phase of cosmological inflation occurred, preceding it and setting it up. Credit : NASA / GSFC 2.) What if the expansion rate and the effects of gravitation were less perfectly balanced? This one is a bit tricky. We normally think of the Universe as a fairly stable place, but that’s only because there are two cosmic properties that have been so well-balanced for so long: the rate at which the Universe expands and the decelerating effects of all the matter and radiation in the Universe. Today, these two effects don’t match, and that’s why we say the expansion of the Universe is accelerating. The fact that there’s a third meaningfully energetic component to the Universe, dark energy, is what causes that mismatch, and therefore is what drives the current accelerated expansion of the cosmos. However, for the first ~6 billion years of the Universe’s history, the expansion rate and the effects of matter-and-radiation didn’t just match, they matched so perfectly well that what we know of as dark energy would have been completely undetectable, even if a hypothetical alien civilization were to develop the exact tools we use today to measure the Universe. The farther back in time you go, the less important dark energy becomes relative to matter and radiation. And we can go back not just billions of years, but all the way back to the first tiny fraction-of-a-second after the hot Big Bang. If the Universe had just a slightly higher matter density (red), it would be closed and have recollapsed already; if it had just a slightly lower density (and negative curvature), it would have expanded much faster and become much larger. The Big Bang, on its own, offers no explanation as to why the initial expansion rate at the moment of the Universe’s birth balances the total energy density so perfectly, leaving no room for spatial curvature at all and a perfectly flat Universe. items.title: The “facts” you learned at school that other countries tell differently
items.summary: “There’s an old expression that goes like this: If you ask a fish about water, the fish will say, ‘What water?’ Because it’s just around them, and a lot of our ideas and assumptions about the world are like that. We just float in them. We’ve never necessarily examined them because it’s sort of obvious.” Last week, I spoke with Jimmy Wales — the man responsible for Wikipedia, the darling of students all over the world since 2001. Our conversation meandered pleasantly over philosophy, technology, cryptocurrency, politics, history, and more. (Big Think members can get first access to watch the full video at this link.) But Wales’s fish parable hit me. What “water” do I swim in? Of course, you can take this two ways. First, the water can be seen broadly: the slightly opaque “ways of thinking” we operate under in the 21st-century post-Enlightenment West. We’ll park that discussion for another day . But we can also see this “water” more practically: What specific facts or pieces of information do I think I know, but aren’t as “obvious” as I thought? I feel as if it’s my philosophical duty to raise doubts where no doubts existed before. And so, here are five “facts” that are actually far more disputed in life — and on Wikipedia — than you might have thought. 1. The Wright brothers invented the airplane Of course! If you’re feeling really bookish, you could add “Kitty Hawk, December 1903.” The story of the Wright brothers is such a Hollywood-ready fact that it’s almost impossible to forget: two bicycle makers, one windy beach, and twelve seconds in the air. Unless you went to school in Brazil. Brazilians have two objections to the Wright brothers’ claim: First, no official watched their 1903 flight. Second, the Wright Flyer needed a rail to take off. So, Brazilians give credit for the airplane’s invention to Alberto Santos-Dumont, who flew his 14-bis biplane near Paris in the autumn of 1906. He did so in public with Aéro-Club officials on hand to measure it, and he took off on his own wheels. Wikipedia doesn’t come down on either side. It has a whole article for the rival claims, where the Wrights and Santos-Dumont have to share the page with Gustave Whitehead, Samuel Langley, and a few other men who were absolutely, definitely first. 2. Alan Turing cracked the Enigma code In 2021, I wrote my book Mini Philosophy , and it was published with three mistakes. First, I wrongly claimed Christopher Nolan directed The Joker . (It was Todd Phillips.) Second, I attributed a quote to Aristotle that actually came from a scholar of Aristotle. But the third mistake, by far and away, was the one that caused the most uproar. I got emails, letters, and pretty intense direct messages. I had claimed the British had cracked the Enigma code. It was Alan Turing and the geniuses of Bletchley Park, surely? That’s what I’d grown up with. But Enigma was first broken in Warsaw at the end of 1932 by a 27-year-old Polish mathematician named Marian Rejewski. That’s almost seven years before the war began. He and his colleagues, Jerzy Różycki and Henryk Zygalski, spent the 1930s reading German messages. Then, in late July 1939 — five weeks before the invasion of Poland — they invited British and French codebreakers to a forest outside Warsaw and showed them how it was done. None of this is a secret. Rejewski’s Wikipedia page sums up what he is known for in a single line: “Solving the Enigma machine cipher.” And GCHQ’s own history is happy to say that the first British Bombe owed a great deal to Turing’s meeting with Polish codebreakers. Turing was still a genius, but he was also standing on Polish shoulders. I mean, really, this fact isn’t so much “disputed” as just “Jonny, you were wrong.” 3. There are seven continents I kind of knew all the other facts on this list before researching this article, but this one was a shock. Seven. There are seven continents. I admit there’s a bit of controversy around “Australia” vs. “Australasia” vs. “Oceania,” but we all agree on seven, right? But in Greece and much of the Romance-speaking world, from Lisbon to Lima, children learn that there are six continents, because North and South America are a single continent called “America.” Russian children learn six as well, but a different six: The Americas stay apart, but Europe and Asia are merged into Eurasia. Something a lot of anthropologists and geologists do as well. And the Olympic flag has five rings for five inhabited continents — one America again, with Antarctica left off altogether until the penguins whip together a bobsled team. The Wikipedia article doesn’t pick a winner. There are, it says, up to seven continents and as few as four. Which means that somewhere, right now, two perfectly well-educated adults are arguing in a pub about something they each learned before they could tie their shoelaces. And they’re both right. 4. The United States won the War of 1812 That depends on who you ask, and in this case, there are three people you could ask. Ask a Canadian, and you’ll hear about a plucky Canada seeing off an American invasion. Ask an American, and it’s the “Second War of American Independence.” Ask a Brit, and you’ll mostly get a blank look because, for Britain, it was a sideshow to the real business of beating Napoleon. And we’ve loved to hate the French ever since. In a 2009 poll, 37% of Canadians said Canada won, and only 9% gave it to the United States. Not every American would argue. “By my count,” the American historian Donald Hickey said, “we lost the War of 1812, and we lost Vietnam.” And Wikipedia? Its editors have spent years on the question. There is a dedicated discussion page titled “Who Won?” and then there was a formal mediation case. And after all that, the article settles on calling the entire debate “inconclusive.” 5. The Second World War began in 1939 On September 1, 1939, Germany invaded Poland. “This country is at war with Germany,” the British Prime Minister, Neville Chamberlain, said at the time. And so, that’s when the Second World War started. But in Russia, the war that matters — the “Great Patriotic War” — began on June 22, 1941, when Germany invaded the Soviet Union. In China, it starts much earlier. In 2017, the Ministry of Education announced that the war against Japan would be counted from 1931, not 1937, and an 8-year war became a 14-year war overnight. Wikipedia keeps a whole archive of editors arguing about this, and at one point, the article itself cited 1937 as the start. My favorite contribution comes from an editor who backed 1939 on entirely practical grounds: They said that if Wikipedia said 1937, a teenager somewhere would copy it into their homework and be marked wrong. Which is, I think, the whole point. So often, the “right” answer is simply the one your teacher is expecting. But both the teacher and the student are stuck in the same problem. As Georg Hegel, Jimmy Wales, and Pink Floyd all knew, we are all just fish swimming in a fishbowl, and no one’s commenting on the water. items.title: What Could Replace the Trump Style of Politics?
items.summary: J onathan Spector’s play Birthright , which had a recent off-Broadway run, crescendos with what can best be described as a Google duel. In the last act, which takes place in 2024, the nearly two-decade bond between a group of American Jewish friends has frayed over Gaza. Izzy, the most left-wing of the bunch, has already abandoned their online group chat, where the friends shared photos of their newborn children, checked in during COVID, and planned their reunions. Thrown together for a funeral, Izzy and another friend, Chaya, begin to argue—as one does these days—about Zionism. They quickly whip out their phones, mustering evidence. “Theodor Herzl colonialism,” Izzy types into the search window, which—in an ingenious bit of stagecraft—appears projected on the wall behind her and starts to flow with online sources. “1930s partition plan Israel,” Chaya counter-Googles. They start scrolling through newspaper articles and Wikipedia pages, hurling raw historical information at each other like malfunctioning robots. But no one is listening. Their friend Noah, watching from the side, offers that going to the internet to prove your point is useless because you’ll invariably find what you’re looking for—“which is why I think this is really, really not a good way to go about having an actual conversation.” This mode of political discourse is surely familiar: the search for a truth that will detonate like an atom bomb, ripping the roof off every other truth. Most of us know that this outcome never, ever happens. But beneath the awareness of information bubbles and fake news, of epistemic breakdown, lies a stubbornly common belief that total victory is achievable. This fantasy has even become its own kind of entertainment—think of Jubilee Media ’s viral videos in which one person has to fend off 20 political opponents like a medieval knight, or the late Charlie Kirk ’s “Prove Me Wrong” college tours. Theories are packed tight with facts and lobbed back and forth in what the German philosopher Hannah Arendt once called “an orgy of truth-telling.” Arendt used this strange phrase in a 1946 letter to the philosopher Gershom Scholem, her dear intellectual sparring partner, after they had gotten into a fierce argument about—what else?—Zionism. One shouldn’t be a “fanatic for truth,” Arendt told him. All this did was harden people in their positions: I have my truth, you have yours, and the only way forward is for you to admit that not just your opinions but your facts are wrong . This is no way to hold a debate, or to conduct politics; all it does is create stasis or even worse. Elsewhere, Arendt called truth in this context “despotic.” She argued instead for a different mode, one that would be surprising—okay, maybe fantastical—to consider today: “an orgy of friendship.” In a recently published book, A World We Share , Roger Berkowitz explores the German philosopher’s thoughts on friendship “as the lens through which she understood politics.” For Arendt, who is best known for her hard-bitten analysis of totalitarianism, friendship might seem to be an uncharacteristically schmaltzy subject, but as filtered through her mind, abstracted and held apart, it sheds all Hallmark associations. Berkowitz, the director of the Hannah Arendt Center for Politics and Humanities at Bard College, provides the material for an intriguing thought experiment, one that might be useful as Americans rub their eyes in the post-midterms dawn. After a decade in which Donald Trump’s tribalist instincts have only accelerated that rush to Google-dueling, it might be worth pursuing Arendt’s idea that friendship, as opposed to truth-telling, is a better model for conducting politics. A rendt never left behind a treatise on friendship, but references to the concept pop up throughout her work and letters. Berkowitz, who has a granular familiarity with her writing, brings all of the strands together. For Arendt, friendship is distinct from love as we often think of it; it is not about losing yourself in order to meld with another person and separate from the rest of the world. Instead, this kind of connection preserves difference and feeds off plurality. Friendship is actually the most worldly of relationships because it forces us to accommodate the separateness of the people we know and care about. [ Read: It’s the morality, stupid ] Arendt articulated three defining features: time spent knowing each other (“a two-week-old friendship does not exist,” she said); talking and more talking and even more talking; and a respect and appreciation for the unique conditions that shape someone else’s worldview. This kind of friendship, she thought, should withstand even the most violent disagreements. “A human being is far more valuable than his opinions,” she wrote in her letter to Scholem, begging that they not lose their connection despite her public disillusionment with the idea of an exclusively Jewish state—a critique Scholem must have felt as a body blow. Berkowitz points out that for Arendt, what makes us human “is not our ability to reason or our grasp of moral certainty or absolute truth but our ability to form lasting and meaningful relationships grounded in mutual recognition and respect.” The fact that she and Scholem had spent more than a decade talking, listening, and yelling was more important to her than any need for them to come to similar conclusions. Her emphasis was rather on this “in-between,” the “common world” they shared and built just by continuing to engage on the issues that mattered to them both. Could any of this possibly be applicable to America’s political culture, which most days resembles the fear and loathing of trench warfare? Dream with me for a minute. Imagine if arguments at Thanksgiving dinner or in Congress proceeded with an awareness that conquering the other person’s worldview was impossible—in the way you can’t really change that old friend who keeps dating the wrong people. Imagine if the goal was to tease out commonalities, instead of trying to will the differences away. This type of politics would be fueled by persuasion, as opposed to force or truth, Berkowitz writes; it would aim “neither at domination nor certainty. It is not about being right.” Arendt’s favored metaphor for this in-between is a table around which people with disparate views and interests sit. The existence of the table matters more than anyone’s particular opinions. The American version of this table does exist, however alienated we may feel from one another. The changing state of the economy, for example, or the future of children’s education, are issues that could potentially be served at this table. Some topics—say, abortion rights—would produce more heat, maybe some fist-pounding. But if the objective is to make sure that the table itself doesn’t evaporate, the conversation might continue. Certain shared worries from our shared world will present themselves as commonalities, even as people’s perspectives remain distinct. Take the proliferation of data centers or the cost of health care. “By talking about what is between them,” Arendt writes, friends and citizens can make that shared world “ever more common.” [ Read: Why we should read Hannah Arendt now ] This is what an orgy of friendship (as opposed to one of truth) could look like. I don’t have any illusions that this shift of mindset is easy.
